metadata.title: Week 1 Progress
metadata.narration_policy: Narration is SCRIPT.md verbatim, one script section per beat.
metadata.visual_policy: Simple illustrative Manim cards in the humanitarians palette. No photos of the fellow, no person icons, no real company or tool logos in the body beats; tools named in the narration are shown as generic drawn icons.
metadata.structure_note: Fellow's chosen simple structure: Claude composer cold open, six body cards, logo outro. No hesitant-writer, verdict or Your Turn beats, because the narration is the fellow's script exactly and the script has no lines for them.
metadata.reformat: full-length; native portrait graphics; preserve source framing

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Keya, and this video is about my first week with Humanitarians AI: who I am, what I learned, and the first video I made. The voice you're hearing is an AI voice reading my script.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hi, Keya'
three result lines land: who I am, what I learned, my first video
the AI-voice disclosure is spoken while the answered composer holds

props.command: Help me share my first week with Humanitarians AI: who I am, what I learned, and the first video I made.

beats.narration_text: I recently graduated with a master's in Software Engineering Systems. I've mostly worked in software development, as an automation developer, with Java, Python, AWS, SQL, Selenium and JUnit.

shot.visual_intent: A degree card, then an automation developer's toolkit drawn as generic icons (no logos), each landing on its spoken name.

show.event: a diploma card draws in: 'Master's' over 'Software Engineering Systems'
the card slides up; 'automation developer' lands as the heading
generic icons land one by one on their spoken names: code brackets (Java, Python), cloud (AWS), database (SQL), browser with cursor (Selenium), checklist (JUnit)
a line links the icons into one automated test pipeline

beats.narration_text: My last graduate project was VeriCode, a collaborative code review platform. I owned the review lifecycle: a state machine that moves a pull request through five states, with undo, and a rule that stops authors approving their own code.

shot.visual_intent: A generic five-state machine performs itself: a pull request token steps through the states, steps back on undo, then a self-approval arrow is blocked.

show.event: 'VeriCode' and 'collaborative code review' set the scene
five numbered state circles connect left to right, labelled 'the review lifecycle'
a 'pull request' token steps through states 1 to 5
an 'undo' arrow curves back and the token returns one state
an 'author' box sends an arrow to 'approve'; it is blocked with a cross: 'authors can't approve their own code'

beats.narration_text: I joined Humanitarians AI, went to the Monday and Thursday meetups, explored the fellows website, and started learning AI coding with the Brutalist film-as-code workflow.

shot.visual_intent: A one-week strip lights up in narration order: joined, Monday and Thursday meetups, the fellows website, film as code.

show.event: a seven-day week strip draws in, headed 'Week 1'; a 'joined' marker drops at the start
Monday and Thursday light up as 'meetup'
a generic browser window opens labelled 'fellows website'
a film strip and a code bracket join as 'film as code'

beats.narration_text: Brutalist builds a video from code. A beat sheet describes every moment. The narration is generated first, and its timing drives every animation. Quality checks test layout, text and facts before anything is final.

shot.visual_intent: The pipeline performs itself with this film's own files: a real beat-sheet excerpt, this beat's measured narration length, animation bars snapping to it, then three checks.

show.event: 'code' becomes 'video': a bracket morphs into a play triangle
a code card shows real lines from this film's beat_sheet.json
a narration waveform draws first, with its measured length
animation bars stretch to match the waveform's length
three checks tick in turn: layout, text, facts; then 'final'

beats.narration_text: My first video explains how AI draws the frames between an animator's drawings, and why anime is so hard for it. I was completely new to AI coding, so everything took time to understand, and the week was full of issues to work through.

shot.visual_intent: Two key drawings with in-betweens filling, as in the first video; then issue cards from the fellow's own frictional log stack up and are worked through one by one.

show.event: 'How AI Draws Anime Frames': two key drawings (plain stars) with empty slots between
the in-between slots fill in
'new to AI coding' lands; issue cards stack up: a mispronounced name, failed quality gates, portrait layouts
each issue card gets a check mark in turn

beats.narration_text: For me, coding with AI is a new bridge I'm walking across, and I'm excited to keep learning and gain more knowledge along the way.

shot.visual_intent: A bridge arcs between two banks; a dot of footsteps crosses it (no person icon) while 'keep learning' lands on the far side.

show.event: two banks: 'software engineering' and 'coding with AI'
a bridge arc draws between them
footsteps advance along the bridge, about halfway
'keep learning' lands on the far bank as the steps continue

beats.narration_text: Week 1 Progress. Built with Claude, for Humanitarians AI.

show.event: the Humanitarians AI mark springs in
the @HumanitariansAI handle settles beneath it
